_comment: Unit 3's batch. Same rules as voice_curate.json.
Unit 3's yap is mostly commentary on the unit's own shape: which sections a list
points at, which example to follow closely, what to practise. One entry fixes a
heading that the audit could not see on its own - '3.0 Time in distributed systems
— the problem this unit solves' - because the heading is glued to the sentence
before it by the sentence splitter, so the tell was reported against that sentence.

edits.why: the fact is about a crashed node, not about what the reader should note
edits.find: Note the word active — a crashed node keeps its high number but cannot win.
edits.to: A crashed node keeps its high number but cannot win.

edits.why: 'two points about this unit matter' announces the paragraph instead of making the point; the four requirements are the point
edits.find: Two points about this unit matter. Every algorithm here answers to the four requirements in 3.3.2 — safety, liveness, fairness and, for mutual exclusion, the number of messages. Those four turn a list of algorithms into a comparison.
edits.to: Every algorithm here answers to the four requirements in 3.3.2 — safety, liveness, fairness and, for mutual exclusion, the number of messages — and those four are what turn a list of algorithms into a comparison.

edits.why: 'matter more here than anywhere else in the course' compares this unit with the others; the examples are the content, and 'what to practise' is advice about reading
edits.old: Worked examples matter more here than anywhere else in the course: the Lamport timestamp, the Bully election and the Ricart–Agrawala example all apply a rule to specific messages or processes, so the arithmetic is what to practise.
edits.new: The Lamport timestamp, the Bully election and the Ricart–Agrawala example all apply a rule to specific messages or processes.

edits.why: the heading has to name the subject; which unit solves it is the unit's own title, one line above
edits.find: .0 Time in distributed systems — the problem this unit solves

edits.why: a sentence whose whole content is which sections the list above points at
edits.old: Note how the last three point straight at 3.3 and 3.4 of this unit.

edits.why: 'this section and 3.2 belong together' is a comment on the notes' structure; that Lamport timestamps cannot make the decision is the fact
edits.old: That decision is exactly what Lamport timestamps cannot make (they order everything, and prove nothing about concurrency) and vector clocks can, which is why this section and 3.2 belong together.
edits.new: Lamport timestamps cannot make that decision — they order everything and prove nothing about concurrency — and vector clocks can.

edits.why: 'the RTT correction above' points at the page; the correction in the formula is the fact
edits.old: which is exactly what the RTT correction above is doing.
edits.new: which is what the RTT correction in the formula is doing.

edits.why: an instruction on how to work through the algorithms, wrapped around a fact that survives it
edits.old: So when you assess the algorithms in this unit — the central coordinator (3.3.4), Lamport's and Ricart–Agrawala's permission schemes, and the token ring (3.3.5) — run each against these four requirements in order and name what it costs to satisfy them. The cost is almost always a message count, which is what makes the comparison worth drawing.
edits.new: Each of the algorithms — the central coordinator (3.3.4), Lamport's and Ricart–Agrawala's permission schemes and the token ring (3.3.5) — satisfies the four requirements at a cost, and that cost is almost always a message count.

edits.why: the make failure is the content; that it is the one to quote is advice about answering
edits.find: The classic failure, and the one to quote when a question asks for a consequence of clock skew: in Unix, the make command is used to compile new or modified code without recompiling unchanged code.
edits.to: The classic failure is in Unix, where the make command is used to compile new or modified code without recompiling unchanged code.

edits.why: the paragraph already shows why the estimate is an estimate; a sentence saying it is the part worth understanding adds nothing
edits.old: This is the part worth understanding, because it shows why the estimate is an estimate.

edits.why: 'what matters is' rates the sentence instead of stating it
edits.find: What matters is the internal consistency of the clocks, not whether they are close to real time.
edits.to: The clocks only have to be internally consistent; they need not be close to real time.

edits.why: 'the distinction worth writing down' is advice; the distinction itself is the content
edits.old: , and that is the distinction worth writing down:

edits.why: 'the one to follow closely' rates the example; what the example shows is the content
edits.old: The first ring example is the one to follow closely, because it shows

edits.find: The four sub-topics are stages of one argument rather than four separate topics.
edits.why: a sentence about how the sub-topics relate to each other; the four sentences that follow say what each one does

edits.find: The reading order is the order to work through: agreement on time, then ordering without time, then using the ordering, then choosing a leader.
edits.why: reading-order advice, and the same order is already the order of the sections

edits.find: Every algorithm here answers to the four requirements in 3.3.2 — safety, liveness, fairness and, for mutual exclusion, the number of messages — and those four are what turn a list of algorithms into a comparison.
edits.to: Every algorithm here answers to the same four requirements — safety, liveness, fairness and, for mutual exclusion, the number of messages.
edits.why: the requirements are the content; the section number is navigation and the clause about turning a list into a comparison rates the notes instead of teaching
